## The question

At the time of writing, it is a few weeks before the Autumn Internationals 2026. For the Southern Hemisphere teams, this will conclude their 2025-2026 season, with teams looking ahead to the 2027 season. In comparison, the Northern Hemisphere teams are just beginning their season, with the Six Nations coming in February. Ahead of the 2027 Men's Rugby World Cup in Australia, unions and head coaches around the world will be deliberating over their squad make up.Selecting a World Cup squad means trading experience against form and fitness. Coaches have to decide how many proven internationals to take, how much to trust players with few caps, and where in the team each of those choices matters. Those decisions are usually argued from opinion. This project puts evidence behind one part of them.

**Primary question:** what separated Rugby World Cup semi-finalists from beaten quarter-finalists (2015–2023) in the international test experience of the players they gave minutes to?

**Secondary question:** where in the team did that difference sit, by position group?

**Case study:** how did the Wales squad that reached the 2019 semi-final compare with the squad that went out in the 2023 quarter-final?

::: {.callout-tip title="Method decision: compare with the beaten quarter-finalists, not the whole field"}
Comparing the 12 semi-finalists with all 48 other teams mostly shows that strong teams have experienced players. Comparing them with the 12 teams they beat in the quarter-finals is a harder, fairer test. Every team in it was good enough to get out of its pool, so the comparison is between the last four and the last eight. Pool exits are still shown, but they are left out of the test.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Method decision: weight by minutes, not by squad list"}
A 33-man squad includes players who barely played. Every team-level measure here is weighted by the World Cup minutes each player actually played, so it reflects whom the coaches trusted on the pitch, not whom they named.
:::

## Building the dataset

Neither source offers a download, so the dataset was scraped and assembled from scratch. It was worth noting, this was built by Claude due to lack of experience of scraping.

| Source | What it provides |
|------------------------------------|------------------------------------|
| Wikipedia squad pages ([2015](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Rugby_World_Cup_squads), [2019](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_Rugby_World_Cup_squads), [2023](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Rugby_World_Cup_squads)) | Every squad member's position, date of birth, career caps and club, as of each tournament's first day. Injury call-ups are marked. |
| [all.rugby](https://all.rugby) player pages | Every test and club match since 2013/14, with competition, opponent, shirt number and minutes played. |

**Scraping politely.** Requests went through `httr2` with a small politeness layer: every request identifies the project and a contact address, paths disallowed by the site's robots.txt are refused, requests are at least three seconds apart (longer if robots.txt asks), and temporary failures are retried. Every page was cached as raw HTML on its first request, so a rerun never hits the site twice.

**Validation.** Four checks ran before any analysis:

1.  **Dates.** all.rugby gives match dates as day and month only, so years were rebuilt from the season label. Every World Cup match had to fall inside its tournament's dates. \[TBC: result\]
2.  **Minutes.** Player minutes were added up per team per match; each total should be close to 15 × 80 plus stoppage time. \[TBC: number of team-matches flagged, and how they were fixed\]
3.  **Name matching.** Wikipedia and all.rugby spell names differently (accents, initials, nicknames). Players were matched on exact normalised name, then on first initial and surname, then by hand. \[TBC: share of minutes matched\]
4.  **Coverage.** Teams whose players showed almost no test minutes were checked by hand, to catch missing data that would look like inexperience. \[TBC\]

The final dataset has \[TBC\] player-tournaments from 60 team-tournaments: 20 teams at each of three World Cups. Three 2019 pool matches were cancelled because of Typhoon Hagibis, so 141 matches were played.

::: {.callout-tip title="Method decision: test matches only"}
all.rugby covers the major club leagues well but not every domestic league. Romanian club rugby, for example, is missing. Those gaps sit with the teams that went out early, so treating missing club minutes as zero would make those teams look inexperienced because of the data, not the players. Test matches are covered for every nation, so the primary analysis uses international experience only. Club minutes are the next step (see [What next](#what-next)).
:::

## Measuring experience

Each player gets two measures for each tournament:

-   **Career caps** at the start of the tournament: long-term international depth.
-   **Recent test minutes:** minutes played in tests in the two years before the tournament. A test against a tier 2 opponent counts 0.7 of a tier 1 test.

$$
\text{recent test experience}_i = \sum_{m \,\in\, \text{tests, 2 years}} \text{minutes}_{i,m} \times w_{\text{opp}(m)}, \qquad w = \begin{cases} 1.0 & \text{tier 1 opponent} \\ 0.7 & \text{tier 2 opponent} \end{cases}
$$

Each team is then summarised by its minutes-weighted average, so a player's contribution is in proportion to the minutes he played at the tournament:

$$
\bar{x}_{\text{team}} = \frac{\sum_i \text{WC minutes}_i \times x_i}{\sum_i \text{WC minutes}_i}
$$

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Recent test experience (from the project's utils)"
test_experience <- function(gamesheets, tournaments, nations,
                            window_years = 2, tier1 = TIER1, tier2_weight = 0.7) {
  tests <- gamesheets |>
    filter(team %in% nations, !is.na(match_date), coalesce(minutes, 0) > 0)

  tournaments |>
    mutate(window_start = start %m-% years(window_years)) |>
    inner_join(tests, by = join_by(window_start <= match_date, start > match_date)) |>
    mutate(opp_weight = if_else(opponent %in% tier1, 1, tier2_weight)) |>
    group_by(tournament, slug) |>
    summarise(test_minutes_2y = sum(minutes),
              test_wmin_2y    = sum(minutes * opp_weight),
              .groups = "drop")
}
```

## Player segments

Two continuous measures describe each player, but coaches think in types: the established international, the newcomer, the veteran who's played little recently. Players were grouped into segments on log caps and log recent test minutes, pooled across all three tournaments so a segment means the same thing in 2015 and 2023. Age was kept out of the segmentation deliberately and described afterwards, to show whether "experienced" simply means "older".

Three approaches were compared:

| Approach | How it works | Strength | Weakness |
|------------------|------------------|------------------|------------------|
| Gaussian mixture model (`mclust`) | Fits elliptical clusters; BIC chooses how many and what shape | Handles correlated, unequal-sized groups; gives each player a probability of belonging | Can create small clusters around the many players with no recent tests |
| k-means | Assigns players to the nearest of *k* centres | Simple and fast | Assumes round clusters of similar size; cuts a correlated cloud at arbitrary points |
| Rule-based quadrants | Fixed cut-points on caps (30) and recent test minutes (the median) | Easiest to explain to coaches | The cut-points are a judgement call |

::: {.callout-tip title="Method decision: how much do the methods agree?"}
If three different methods put players in the same groups, the segments reflect real structure and not one algorithm's assumptions. Agreement was measured with the adjusted Rand index (0 = no better than chance, 1 = identical groupings).

| Pair             | Adjusted Rand index |
|------------------|---------------------|

| GMM vs rules     | \[TBC\]             |

## Where in the team the gap sat

Position groups come from the shirt each player wore in each match, not his listed squad position, so a utility back who started at 13 counts as a centre that week.

| Shirt      | Position group |
|------------|----------------|
| 1–3        | Front row      |
| 4–5        | Lock           |
| 6–8        | Back row       |
| 9–10       | Half-backs     |
| 12–13      | Centres        |
| 11, 14, 15 | Back three     |

Replacements (16–23) were assigned to the group they started in most often over the same two-year window; players with no starts fall back to their Wikipedia position. \[TBC: share of minutes assigned by shirt, by usual position, and from Wikipedia\]

## Limitations

-   **Small numbers.** Twelve semi-finalists against twelve beaten quarter-finalists. The results describe a pattern; they don't predict who will reach a semi-final.
-   **Strength and experience are tangled.** Better teams can select experienced players and also win more. Comparing with beaten quarter-finalists reduces this but doesn't remove it.
-   **Minutes reflect more than selection.** Injuries, cards and the opposition all shape who plays.
-   **Test minutes miss club experience.** A player in the Top 14 or the Champions Cup brings experience this measure doesn't see.
-   **Data starts in 2013/14.** Recent test minutes are complete for every tournament; career caps from Wikipedia cover the longer history.

## What next {#what-next}

The natural extension is **relative experience including club rugby**. Weighting every club minute equally treats a Pro D2 match like a Champions Cup knockout, and fixed weights per competition are only a guess. A better approach:

1.  Rate every club from all.rugby results, using a [Bayesian team-ratings model](../rugby-ratings/index.qmd).
2.  Weight each club minute by the strength of the opposition at the time.
3.  Express experience relative to the squad, or to the opposing matchday 23.

Further steps: a match-level model (does the more experienced matchday 23 win more often than the rankings predict?) and an interactive squad explorer.
